extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of literary criticism; poets and public speakers
extracted.subtask_description: A 19th-century critical essay evaluating the qualities of political oratory and contemporary poetry — identifying virtues and vices of style, substance, delivery, imagination, and moral effect. Useful as prescriptive/evaluative guidance for critics, speakers, and poets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality versus ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: The speaker/writer should not exhaust his mind on 'ornaments of style' or 'an agreeable and imposing selection of topics' at the expense of original thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid merely embellishing what is trite, glossing over what is true, or covering weak sophisms with 'meretricious fancy.' Ornament should not substitute for independent, original observation or strict chains of reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soundness of reasoning (avoid sophistry)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reasoning must be solid and not a 'tissue of glittering sophistry.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rhetorical brilliance that conceals fallacies is criticised—arguments should withstand common-sense scrutiny rather than merely glitter with rhetorical devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity and originality of language
rubrics_metrics.description: Language that is only a 'cento of florid common-places' or 'something second-hand' is defective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer language that is genuinely expressive and original to borrowed, showy, or 'Asiatic redundancy' — avoid clichés and overused classical or parliamentary turns that signal lack of original mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth of principle and strength of passion
rubrics_metrics.description: A good speaker or poet should possess 'steady principles' and 'strong passions' rather than superficial polish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work that lacks conviction or genuine feeling (no steady principles, no strong passions) will be seen as feeble, diffuse, and showy; moral and emotional seriousness matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connection to real life and nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Speeches/poems should allude to objects beyond a confined professional circle; they should not be limited to 'Parliamentary' or classical allusions exclusively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid being so confined to professional or classical reference points that 'not an image has struck his eye' outside the institution; relate to common life and natural incident to give work vitality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Durability and transplantability
rubrics_metrics.description: Style and matter should be lasting — not 'forced' exotics or 'hot-house plants' that won't bear transplanting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works should have strength and stamina, not mere glossiness and gorgeous colour; avoid ephemeral tricks that fail outside their original staged context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity of delivery — extempore versus set speeches
rubrics_metrics.description: Delivery that only 'gives the effect of witty impromptus' but is actually premeditated is less admirable than genuine spontaneous utterance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signs of recitation from memory, 'studied gesture', 'emphatic but monotonous' tone indicate rehearsed, not extemporary, speech. True extempore speech shows varying speed, hesitation, and passion appropriate to the moment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argumentative vigour and willingness to grapple
rubrics_metrics.description: An effective speaker should be able to 'grapple with a powerful antagonist' and contest points directly, not rely on evasive replies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praised is the capacity to overthrow an opponent 'on the spot' and contend 'foot to foot.' Relying on ambushes or prepared magazines of wit to embarrass a forewarned opponent is an inferior tactic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of metaphor and ornament to substance
rubrics_metrics.description: Metaphor, epithets, and ornaments must not mask the hollowness of argument; removed from their setting they should still make sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A harangue 'dazzling with epithets' that becomes 'a paltry string of sophisms' when examined by common sense is a warning: rhetorical splendour must be anchored to sound thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of jargon and scholastic pedantry
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of professional jargon ('House-of-Commons jargon') and pedantic forms of address produces 'pompous inanity' and pleases only 'professional ears.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer clarity and accessibility; avoid formulas ('the Honourable and Learned Gentleman') that fill rhetorical gaps with burlesque self-complacency rather than meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mechanical, rote rhetorical tricks
rubrics_metrics.description: Relying on 'mechanic helps to style' — rote phrases, technical flourishes, and rehearsed tricks — is unworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speeches should not be merely well-turned period pieces recited by rote; such mechanic artifices cheapen content and indicate lack of genuine engagement with the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original wit rather than mere parody
rubrics_metrics.description: True wit requires sense and feeling; being excellent at parody is different from having 'real, original wit.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parody (e.g., imitations and ludicrous imitations) is a skill but not a substitute for original insight; turning serious and affecting matters into farce by lack of sympathy is a defect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency and integrity of political views
rubrics_metrics.description: A valuable public voice should display settled opinion and moral steadiness rather than being 'optional' and picking sides for vanity or convenience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticises speakers who 'pick and chuse' among positions as suits their purpose; integrity (some settled opinion) and moral courage are expected virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity of motives (avoid acting from vanity or self-interest)
rubrics_metrics.description: Positions should not be merely 'dictated by vanity, his interest, or his habits.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rhetoric built on personal vanity or opportunism rather than principle is untrustworthy; assess motives and beware persuasive performance driven by self-interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideological transparency / identifiable core principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Speeches should not merely surround a single hidden watchword (e.g., 'Legitimacy') that explains all variations in tone and policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be transparent about core principles; using varied rhetorical facings to obscure a singular controlling idea that dictates policy makes the orator dangerous and deceptive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral responsibility and public effect of rhetoric
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhetoric has ethical consequences: 'clever men are the tools with which bad men work' and sophistry can serve power to destructive ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should evaluate the social and moral effects of eloquence — not only its polish but whether it abets oppressive power or human suffering (Inquisition, dungeons, war).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of tone and feeling to subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Turning the serious and affecting into farce by removing feeling ('to make any description or sentiment ludicrous, it is only necessary to take away all feeling from it') is a vice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain sympathy and appropriate tone; ridicule of what should arouse sentiment is a failing of character and taste in both speakers and poets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical finish and perfection in poetic execution
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry should demonstrate careful attention to expression: polished lines, modulation of each line 'into the most faultless harmony.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meticulous diction, perfected phrasing, and avoidance of formal faults (false concord, mixed metaphor, imperfect rhyme) are marks of a 'high finisher' in poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between finish and substantive strength
rubrics_metrics.description: Exquisite finish must be balanced by strength and solidity; perfection of execution alone can leave a work wanting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not favor polish at the expense of depth — a poet who 'polishes his lines till they sparkle' but lacks 'strength and solidity' is criticised; aim for both technical excellence and substantial content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of topics and ambitious scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Select topics with daring and caution to suit the ambition of the poet; self-respect should guide the pursuit of popularity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A poet should 'seize on the highest point of eminence' and choose subjects that support true genius; popularity is acceptable only when earned by self-respect and true effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of grossness, vulgarity, and haste
rubrics_metrics.description: Great poetry avoids faults arising from 'grossness, vulgarity, haste, and disregard of public opinion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Labor to avoid coarse workmanship and hurried composition; careful, considered elaboration produces enduring art rather than 'lumbering, feeble, awkward' lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of design and perfection of component parts
rubrics_metrics.description: A work should reconcile 'the integrity of general design with the perfect elaboration of each component part.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for coherent overall structure while also refining every line and image; neither grand design nor minute execution alone suffices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strength of imagery and sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry should exhibit vivid ideal forms and richness of imagery and sentiment: 'vivid ideal forms hover ... over the poet's verse.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-quality imagery (e.g., 'a perfume like that of the magnolia') and genuinely felt sentiment enliven verse; poets who excel in imagery move readers with 'ecstatic union of natural beauty and poetic fancy.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative pacing and mechanical conduction in long poems
rubrics_metrics.description: Long poems must be moved with life and coherence; avoid narratives that 'move slow' or are 'mechanically conducted' like a canal with locks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess pacing and narrative momentum — slow, mechanical progression detracts from effect; aim for a sweeping, natural flow where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalness in diction — avoid affected conceits
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject affected poetic diction and artificial conceits in favour of natural links of beauty: the 'outcry ... against poetic diction and affected conceits' is acknowledged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where poetic diction feels forced or fanciful for its own sake, it reduces effect; allow beauty to arise naturally ('beauty linked to beauty') rather than through mannered conceit.
